analysis.one_liner: Delays the 2015 smog limits and stretches the air-quality review cycle to ten years.
analysis.headline: The House passed the ozone-delay bill 234-177 on June 8, 2016, but the Senate never acted on it before the Congress ended, so the 2015 ozone standards stayed on schedule.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Clean Air Act to postpone the deadlines for the 2015 ground-level ozone (smog) standards, which limit the ozone pollution that power plants, factories, and vehicles produce. It would let states wait until 2024-2026 to designate and plan for the new standard, and would double the review cycle for all air quality standards from every five years to every ten. It would also let the EPA weigh cost and technological feasibility when setting health standards, exempt certain pending construction permits from the new limits, and waive some clean-up requirements in the most polluted areas.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that emit ozone-forming pollution — power plants, refineries, chemical plants, and other large factories — gain the most, because they would get years of extra time before they have to cut emissions. States that had argued the 2015 standard's compliance timeline was unrealistic would also get relief.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Power plants, refineries, and large factories

how_it_helps.text: Delays the deadlines for designating areas and for states to submit implementation plans for the 2015 ozone standards to October 2024, 2025, and 2026, giving polluting facilities years of additional lead time before compliance obligations begin.

Extends the review cycle for all national air quality standards from five years to ten and bars the EPA from completing its next ozone review before October 2025, slowing future tightening of health standards.

Lets the EPA consider technological feasibility as a secondary consideration when setting standards, and exempts permit applications completed or noticed before final designations from the 2015 ozone standards, sparing pending industrial construction projects from the new limits.
Removes the requirement for contingency measures in the most polluted ozone areas and lets cost and economic feasibility be weighed in plan milestones, reducing clean-up obligations.

analysis.who_pays: People who live in areas with unhealthy ground-level ozone — much of it along highways and around industrial corridors — would breathe dirtier air for longer, bearing higher risks of asthma attacks and respiratory illness. The public also loses faster updates to air quality science, since reviews would happen half as often.
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents of areas with smog pollution

drawbacks.text: Delaying the 2015 ozone standards means Americans in nonattainment areas are exposed to ozone concentrations that the EPA's health review found unsafe, with documented respiratory health risks, until the late 2020s.
Doubling the review cycle to ten years means health-based air standards are updated half as often, locking in outdated science for nearly a decade between assessments.

Supporters' best case: states were being asked to meet a new standard on tight timelines with implementation rules not yet written, and designations before guidance existed could force wasteful permitting decisions; the bill addresses that by requiring rules and guidance to be issued together with any new standard.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The procedural improvements (issuing implementation guidance alongside new standards) are reasonable on their own, but the bill's core effect is an eight-to-ten-year delay of health protections that were already finalized in 2015, in exchange for compliance savings for large emitters. The costs fall on people's lungs, not on budgets, which is hard to justify against the modest administrative savings.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote on June 8, 2016, but the Senate simply referred it to its Environment and Public Works Committee on June 9 and it never came up again before the Congress ended, so it never became law.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2016, with 43 cosponsors (40 Republicans, 3 Democrats), and cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee on a 30-23 vote in May 2016.
On June 8, 2016, the House passed the bill 234-177, with Republicans voting 227-10 in favor and Democrats 7-167 against.
A Democratic motion to send the bill back to committee with instructions to strip the ozone-rule delay failed 173-239 the same day, with all but two Republicans voting no.

The Senate received the bill on June 9, 2016, and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where it stayed for the rest of the 114th Congress without a committee vote or floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in a Senate committee, the 2015 ozone standards stayed on their original schedule and residents of smog-affected areas kept the protection the bill would have delayed; large emitters avoided getting the added grace period they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Smog-affected residents kept the 2015 standards on schedule

for.name: Rep. Pete Olson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to delay implementation of the 2015 ozone standards and slow future reviews.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill amended on a 30-23 vote in May 2016 and moved it to the House floor.

for.name: 227 of 245 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, 227-10, providing the votes to pass the bill.

for.name: Fossil fuel and manufacturing trade associations
for.what_they_did: Backed delay of the 2015 ozone standard, which the Obama EPA had finalized over industry objections about compliance costs.

against.name: Rep. Bobby Rush
against.role: Ranking member, House Energy Subcommittee on Energy and Power
against.what_they_did: Offered amendments in committee and moved to recommit the bill with instructions to repeal the ozone-rule delay if implementing it would raise health risks; the motion failed 173-239.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 9, 2016, and never reported the bill or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party: Republicans voted 227-10 yes while Democrats voted 7-167 no, though the bill had three Democratic cosponsors and committee Democrats forced votes against it.

industries.industry: Power plants and fossil fuel producers
industries.note: The bill would have delayed by years their obligation to cut the ozone-forming emissions the 2015 standard targets, and exempted pending permit applications from the new limits. The savings in compliance costs would come at the expense of cleaner air for people living near these facilities.

industries.industry: Heavy manufacturers and industrial permit applicants
industries.note: Construction and expansion permits in the pipeline would be exempt from the 2015 ozone standards, and the most polluted areas would no longer need contingency clean-up measures. The public bears the resulting pollution exposure.

States would get several more years to prepare designations and implementation plans and would no longer face reviews on a five-year cycle. Some states, however, had already begun compliance work, and the bill authorizes no additional funds to carry out its own new requirements and studies.

The agency's authority to review health standards every five years, set standards based on health without weighing feasibility, and require contingency measures in extreme nonattainment areas would all be curtailed. Its weakened position runs directly against the public's interest in timely health protection.
